1.1–2 Vasiṣṭha, the best among those skilled in speech, unsurpassed and knowing the three periods of time; one who knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, fully established in yogic practices;
one who is devoted to the welfare of all beings, peaceful, true to his word, and free from weariness.
1.2cd One who recognizes virtue in all beings and whose sole purpose is the welfare of others.
One who has conquered the senses, conquered anger, knows the Veda, is dear to Brahmins,
has retired to a penance grove, is gentle, and is ever devoted to Vedic study.
It was well-served by highly fortunate Brahmins who were knowers of Brahman,
and it was constantly devoted to dharma, always performing its morning rites.
Having prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before the Sage of Great Compassion,
Śakti, filled with faith and with palms joined in reverence, questioned his father.
Śakti said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all scriptures, devoted to the welfare of all beings!
By what means may one [be liberated] from this cycle of existence, which is overwhelmed by manifold sufferings?"

1.7ab How might I, whose mind is blinded by intoxication, obtain knowledge and be liberated from this world filled with various fears and possessed of birth, death, and old age? 1.7cd How might I, whose mind is blinded by intoxication, obtain knowledge and be liberated from this world filled with various fears and possessed of birth, death, and old age?
1.8ab Thus questioned by his son Śakti, who was a proponent of the Vedas,
1.8cd the seer, looking with both eyes, spoke these words:
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Arise, arise, may it be well with you, Śakti, best among the wise!
I shall tell you the eternal means that grants happiness and destroys worldly existence."
1.10 Having spoken thus, the blessed yogi Vasiṣṭha, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman,
sang of the god Nārāyaṇa who dwells in the hearts of all beings.
1.11 I shall describe the god who is the source of the world, the object of meditation for yogis, and the stainless one.
Blissful, undecaying, eternal, the supreme bliss, the Lord.
Having bowed to Hṛṣīkeśa, the Lord of the World, with a well-composed mind,
he gazed upon Śakti with his eyes and spoke this out of compassion:
1.13ab Come, come, O tiger among sages, you who are devoted to your guru and have conquered your senses!
1.13cd Listen to that which was previously spoken by Brahmā, which grants me liberation.
1.14ab Seated comfortably in the lotus posture, the four-faced, imperishable one;
1.14cd the creator of all things moving and unmoving, Brahmā, the Supreme Lord. Having gone there at one time, I praised him with hymns and bowed down.
1.15cd He asked this very same matter about which you are questioning me.
O God of gods, Lord of the world, four-faced one with the excellent countenance! Confused by many scriptures and with a wandering mind, I am lost in delusion.
1.17ab O Blessed One, by what means may I go to that ultimate, supreme state?
1.17cd Tell me that secret, blissful, and ageless state, O Grandfather.
1.18ab Thus addressed by me, the Self-Existent One, the Leader of the World, was satisfied;
1.18cd seeing me with a very gracious mind, he spoke this out of compassion:
1.19ab For one who is born, two paths enjoined by the Veda are to be known;
1.19cd both of these consist of action: the impelling and the restraining.
1.20ab For the castes and stages of life, action preceded by desire and volition is indeed the impeller;
1.20cd for it is that which sets one in motion within saṃsāra.
That very same [knowledge], when conjoined with wisdom and devoid of all desires,
becomes the cause of cessation, because it brings about the cessation of rebirth.
The wise know that within the Vedas there are two kinds of means for turning [the mind away from worldly objects], each being a means to liberation: the external and the internal.
1.23ab That which is external consists of outward action; thus it is the prescribed means. 1.23cd But the internal [means] is performed within oneself by the intellect alone, through the intellect.
1.24ab One should perform the daily rites within those two according to the prescribed rule;
1.24cd endowed with knowledge and devotion, one shall always attain eternal bliss.
Whether one is wise or ignorant, as long as there is a means of maintaining the body,
so long must the action prescribed for one's caste and stage of life be performed for the sake of liberation.
Having thus taught in truth the entire essence of ritual action and the section on rites (karmakāṇḍa), Brahmā then himself became established in yoga.
1.27ab Since even the wise who seek liberation perform action alone,
1.27cd therefore you too, O best of Brahmins, perform that action with knowledge.
1.28 Having heard this spoken by Vasiṣṭha, the son Śakti, unwearied,
spoke again to the best of sages, being self-restrained and endowed with faith.
Śakti said:
"O best of Brahmins, you have stated that liberation belongs to one who performs the action prescribed by the Vedas together with knowledge. Of these two, O Lord, tell me about knowledge."
1.30ab Thus addressed by his own son, Vasiṣṭha, with a delighted mind, 1.30cd gazed upon his son with both eyes and spoke to him, who was the very embodiment of knowledge.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Know that knowledge has yoga as its essence, and yoga abides within the self.
That yoga is endowed with eight limbs; it is called the universal dharma.
1.32ab I shall correctly explain the constituent parts according to my wisdom and as I have heard them. 1.32cd Having become most composed, listen, O son of noble vows.
1.33ab Restraint (yama) and observance (niyama), as well as posture (āsana), are desired;
1.33cd breath control (prāṇāyāma), as well as withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) and concentration (dhāraṇā);
1.33ef meditation (dhyāna) and absorption (samādhi)—these, O one whose wealth is austerity, are the limbs of yoga.
1.34ab First, there are four external [elements], followed by the internal ones.
1.35ab The restraints (yamas) are said to be tenfold, and likewise the observances (niyamas) are ten.
1.35cd Likewise, there are ten among all the postures (āsanas) that are the most excellent.
1.35ef Among those, O son, four are the most excellent—the paths to liberation.
1.36ab Prāṇāyāma is said to be threefold, and pratyāhāra is fourfold.
1.37ab Dhāraṇā is said to be fivefold; dhyāna is proclaimed to be sixfold.
1.37cd Samādhi is said to be equanimity (samatā), as long as dhyāna remains distinct [from it].
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, fortitude, forbearance, compassion, straightforwardness, moderation in diet, and purity—these are the ten *yamas*. (Śrī Padmasaṃhitā 1.38)
1.39ab Through action, mind, or speech, toward all beings at all times;
1.39cd the non-production of affliction is declared by the yogis as "non-violence" (ahiṃsā).
1.40ab If non-violence were that which is enjoined by scriptural injunction, there would be no harming of living beings.
1.40cd For even when prescribed by injunction, there is violence, such as in rituals like *abhicāra* (malevolent magic).
Truth is said to be that which is beneficial to living beings and speech uttered according to what is right;
and truth is also said to be that which is pleasant. This truth I declare to you.
1.42ab Being free from longing for all material things by deed, mind, or speech—
1.42cd this is declared as non-stealing (asteya) by the sages who perceive the truth.
1.43ab Through action, mind, and speech, toward all beings at all times;
1.43cd the renunciation of sexual intercourse in every respect is declared to be *brahmacarya*.

1.44ab Engaging with one’s own wife according to the prescribed rule during each fertile season, 1.44cd and practicing celibacy— this is declared to be the conduct for those dwelling in the householder stage of life.
And constant service to the teacher is declared to be celibacy (brahmacarya).
1.46ab In the loss of wealth, or even in separation from kinsmen or prosperity;
1.46cd and in their acquisition—in all such cases, the steadying of the mind is fortitude (dhṛti).
That state of equanimity which embodied beings maintain toward all things pleasant and unpleasant is declared by the learned exponents of the Vedas to be patience.
Whether toward another, or toward one's circle of kinsmen, or toward a friend or an enemy— at whatever [object] the thought of compassion always abides, that is proclaimed as *dayā* (compassion).
1.49ab Regarding those other [actions] prescribed for the mind, speech, and body,
whether they involve engagement or withdrawal, 1.49cd having a single, uniform nature is straightforwardness (*ārjava*).

Eight mouthfuls are prescribed for a sage, sixteen for forest-dwellers, and thirty-two for householders; for students, there is no fixed limit. This is said to be moderate eating; for others, it is eating little.
1.51ab Purity is said to be twofold: external as well as internal.
1.51cd External purity is traditionally held to consist of earth and water; internal purity is the purification of the mind.
1.51ef And the purification of the mind is to be understood through dharma and the science of the self (adhyātmavidyā).
1.52ab The ten restraints (yamas), beginning with non-violence, have been declared to you by me out of affection and because of your devotion.
Austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the Lord,
listening to the established doctrines, modesty, intelligence, recitation, and vows—
these are declared to be the tenfold observances (niyamas). Listen now to each of them individually.
1.54ab By means of the path prescribed by rule, such as the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances;
1.54cd they say that the purification of the body is the highest austerity among all austerities.
1.55 "The mind of men should be content with whatever comes by chance"—this is what the sages call steadfastness; they declare that contentment is the defining characteristic of happiness.
1.56ab Trust in both dharma and adharma is called āstikya.
Wealth, grain, or anything else that is given by one endowed with faith to those in distress, having been acquired through righteous means— this is proclaimed as *dāna* (charitable giving).
1.58ab That worship of Viṣṇu with a serene disposition,
as well as 1.58cd worship performed correctly with devotion— this is the worship of the Lord.
1.59 A heart free from passion, speech free from falsehood and the like,
and a body free from violence and other such acts— this is the worship of the Lord.

1.60ab The hearing of the established doctrine (siddhānta-śravaṇa) has been declared, as well as the contemplation of Vedānta. = Ahirbudhnya 31.25cd 1.61ab The study of one’s own Vedic branch (svakīya-śākhā), as well as the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
1.61cd and likewise, the hearing of the established doctrine regarding whatever else has been studied.
Whatever action may be contemptible within the paths of the Vedas, the world,
or the [social] conventions, the sense of shame felt toward such an act is proclaimed as *hrī*.
1.63ab And regarding all that has been prescribed, whatever understanding may arise through faith; 1.63cd and whatever is external to what has been taught by the Guru, one should avoid that.

1.64ab The practice of mantra through the path prescribed by rule is known as *japa*. Ahirbudhnya 31.29d 1.64cd And *japa* is declared to be of two kinds: that which is whispered (*upāṃśu*) and that which is mental (*mānasa*).

1.65ab Recitation that is whispered is said to be a thousand times more effective than loud recitation; 1.65cd And mental recitation is even more excellent, being a thousand times superior to that as well.
1.66ab When previously instructed by a gracious teacher, with his permission,
1.66cd the undertaking of means for the sake of accomplishing dharma, artha, and kāma is called a vow (vrata).
1.67ab I shall also describe the postures; listen with a concentrated mind, my son.
1.67cd Svastika, Gomukha, Padma, Vīra, and likewise Siṃhāsana;
1.67ef Māyūra, Kukkuṭa, Kūrma, and likewise Bhadrāsana.
1.67gh Likewise, I shall describe individually the characteristics of their liberated posture (muktāsana).
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs,
sitting with the body straight— this they call the *svastika* posture.
1.69ab Placing the two ankles upon the sides of one's own perineum, with the feet [turned upward],
1.69cd this is called the Svastika posture, which destroys all sins.
One should place the right ankle on the left side of the back;
likewise, one should place the left ankle on the right side. This they call Gomukha.
1.71ab One should bind the two big toes with the hands in a reverse manner;
1.71cd placing both soles of the feet upon the thighs, O best of Brahmins,
1.71ef this becomes the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is honored by all.
Placing one foot upon one thigh and likewise the other thigh upon the other [thigh], this is declared to be the vīrāsana posture.
1.73ab One should place the two ankles below the scrotum, on both sides of the perineal seam;
1.73cd the right ankle with the left, and the other with the right.
Placing the hands on the knees and extending the fingers of one's own body,
with the mouth open, one should gaze at the tip of the nose, well-composed.
This shall be the lion-throne, always worshipped by yogins.
1.76ab Pressing the earth firmly with the palms of both hands,
1.76cd and placing the elbows of the two arms at the sides of the navel;
1.77ab With the head and feet raised, one stands like a staff in the air.
1.77cd This, indeed, is the peacock posture (mayūrāsana), which destroys all evils.

1.78ab Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), with the hands placed between the knees and the thighs, 1.78cd and having settled them upon the ground, one establishes the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana) situated in the void.
Placing the two ankles below the scrotum and on either side of the perineal seam,
and firmly binding the feet against the sides with both hands so that they are perfectly motionless—
this shall be the Bhadrasana posture, which removes all diseases and poisons. (Padmasaṃhitā 1.79)
1.80ab Having blocked the anus with the two ankles in reverse order, being well-composed;
1.80cd this is known as the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana), so say those who know yoga.
1.81ab Having placed one ankle above the penis and likewise [the other] above [it],
1.81cd and having inserted the space between the ankles [underneath], this is known as the *muktāsana*.
Having pressed the subtle *sīvanī* [tendon] on the left side with the left ankle,
and likewise the right [side] with the right ankle— this is the *muktāsana*.

1.83ab Endowed with the restraints (yama), the observances (niyama), and the postures (āsana), 1.83cd and having performed the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śuddhi), you should then practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
1.84ab For one who performs all the limbs of yoga, such as breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the rest,
1.84cd his exertion will be in vain if he does not effect the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śuddhi).
Thus ends the first chapter in the Yoga Section of the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā.
The second chapter:
Śakti said:

2.1ab O Blessed One, my father, tell me according to the prescribed rule about the purification of the channels (*nāḍī*). 2.1cd By what means do the channels of all embodied beings become purified? 2.2ab [Tell me] also the origin of the channels and their maintenance according to the rule.
2.2cd What is the nature of the bulb (kanda) said to be, and how many winds (vāyu) reside there?

2.3ab Furthermore, the locations and the individual functions of the vital airs (vāyu) within this body must be understood, O best among embodied beings. 2.3cd You ought to explain these according to their true nature, for there is no knower of them other than you.
2.4ab Thus addressed by Śakti, the yogi, his mind fully absorbed in that [state], 2.4cd looked upon his own son with compassion and recounted all of that.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O twice-born one, know that the body of all living beings consists of ninety-six finger-breadths measured by their own fingers."
2.6ab There are thirty-two bones in the body, including those of the two sides of the spinal column; 2.6cd and seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs) are likewise situated therein.
2.7ab The vital breath (prāṇa) is superior to the body and measures twelve finger-breadths.
2.7cd Because the wind (vāyu) departs [from the body], it is therefore called "prāṇa."
2.8ab In the center of the body is the seat of fire, with the luster of molten gold.
2.8cd For humans it is triangular, and for quadrupeds it is square. 2.8ef For birds it is circular; I tell you this as the truth.
2.9ab But in the midst of that, the slender flame of fire always abides.
2.9cd If you wish to hear where the center of the body is, listen.
Two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis,
one finger-breadth between those two is declared to be the center of the body.
2.11ab There is a bulb (kanda) in this body, nine finger-breadths from the center of the body;
2.11cd it is four finger-breadths in height and likewise in length.
2.12ab Its form is like that of an egg, adorned with skin and bone;
2.12cd its center is called the navel, from which the wheel arises.
2.13ab The body is a wheel endowed with twelve spokes; by it [the self] is established.
2.13cd In this wheel, the individual soul (jīva) revolves, impelled by merit and demerit.
Just as a weaver moves within the midst of a web of threads,
so does this vital breath (prāṇa) move downward within this root-cakra of the individual soul (jīva).

2.15ab The *jīva* is always more firm than the *prāṇa* within all bodies; for that which moves mounted upon the *prāṇa* is the *jīva*, and without it, [the *prāṇa*] does not exist. 2.15cd Above that is the location of the *kuṇḍalinī*, situated transversely and below the navel.
2.16ab This [Kuṇḍalinī], consisting of the eightfold nature, is coiled eight times.
2.16cd Beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *kṣa*, she is designated as "Kuṇḍalinī.
2.16ef Having properly restrained the movement of the vital air (*vāyu*), she remains forever established [therein].
2.17ab Having likewise enveloped the opening of the *brahmarandhra* with her mouth,
2.17cd at the time of yoga, she is awakened together with the fire by means of the *apāna*.
2.18ab Throbbing from the space of the heart, in the form of a serpent, intensely radiant;
2.18cd dancing eternally in the space of the hearts of yogins, the middle channel (madhyamā);
2.18ef by means of the bliss of the wind itself, the breath then enters the *suṣumṇā*.
2.19ab The channel situated in the middle of the *kanda* is celebrated as the *suṣumṇā*.
2.19cd All [other channels] reside around this wheel known as the *nāḍi*.
2.20ab Furthermore, O son, among all the channels, fourteen are the principal ones.
2.21ab After that, Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Sarasvatī.
2.22ab Kuhū, Varaṇā, and the illustrious Saptamī;
2.22cd Pūṣā, Payasvinī, and likewise Śaṅkhinī as the tenth.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, and likewise Viśvodarā are recorded;
Alambuṣā and these others are the fourteen principal ones among them all.
Among them, three are the most prominent; among those three, one is considered supreme.
On the path to liberation, that is Suṣumṇā, blazing and the sustainer of the universe.
2.25ab O son, in the middle of the bulb (kanda), the suṣumṇā is well-established.
2.25cd Together with the bone situated in the middle of the back, it always resides at the crown of the head.
2.26ab That Suṣumṇā is proclaimed as the path to liberation, located at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
2.26cd It is to be known as unmanifest (avyaktā), subtle, and is remembered as belonging to Viṣṇu (vaiṣṇavī).
2.27ab Both Iḍā and Piṅgalā are on her left and right respectively.
2.27cd Iḍā is situated on her left, and Piṅgalā is situated on the right.
2.28ab The Moon and the Sun move within the Iḍā and the Piṅgalā.
2.28cd The Moon is to be known as being in the Iḍā; the Sun is traditionally said to be in the Piṅgalā.

2.29ab The moon is said to be of the nature of *tamas*, while the sun is said to be of the nature of *rajas*. 2.29cd These two alone sustain the entirety of time, consisting of night and day. 2.30ab The *suṣumṇā* is the enjoyer of time; this is declared to be the secret.
2.31ab Sarasvatī and Kuhū are situated on the two sides of Suṣumṇā.
2.31cd Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā are on the back and front of Iḍā.
2.31ef Pūṣā and Yaśasvinī are on the back and front of Piṅgalā.
2.32ab Viśvodarā is situated between Kuhū and Hastijihvā;
2.32cd Varaṇā is established between Yaśasvinī and Kuhū.
2.33ab And between Pūṣā and Sarasvatī stands Payasvinī;
2.33cd and between Gāndhārī and Sarasvatī stands Śaṅkhinī.
2.34ab O best of Brahmins, the Alambuṣā is situated below the center of the kanda.
2.34cd On the eastern side of the Suṣumṇā, the Kuhū is situated as far as the penis.
2.35ab The all-pervading Vāraṇā is to be known as extending both downwards and upwards;
2.35cd and the Yaśasvinī is held to extend from [the heart] to the big toe of the right foot.
2.36ab Know, O son, that Piṅgalā goes upward to the end of the southern nostril;
2.36cd Pūṣā is in the south, and Netrā is behind Piṅgalā.
2.37ab And the Payasvinī, O best of Brahmins, is held to extend as far as the ears in the south;
2.37cd likewise, the Sarasvatī is established upwards from the tongue.
2.38ab O Brahmin-sage, the Śaṅkhinī has ascended upwards from the left ear;
2.38cd the Gāndhārī is situated behind the Iḍā, reaching as far as the corner of the left eye.
2.39ab The *iḍā* is considered to extend to the left nostril, while the *piṅgalā* is held to be on the right.
2.39cd *Jayā* is to be known as situated in the left portion, and *pūṣā* is likewise established there.
2.39ef *Hastijihvā* is likewise maintained to extend to the big toe of the left foot.
2.40ab The channel known as Viśvodarā is said to extend everywhere on the left side.
2.40cd Alambuṣā is on the left part, extending downward from the base of the anus.
2.41ab Other channels arise from these, and yet others arise from those as well;
2.41cd just as on the leaf of a *aśvattha* tree, so it should be understood regarding all the channels.
2.42ab Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
2.42cd nāga, kūrma, kṛkaraka, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
2.43ab These ten winds move through all the channels (nāḍīs). 2.43cd Among these, five winds—prāṇa and the others—are considered primary.
2.44ab Among these, the most principal is *prāṇa*, which is established below the *kanda*.
2.44cd It moves in the mouth, the two nostrils, the heart, and the region of the navel;
2.44ef that *prāṇa* also resides in the big toe and in these other places as well.
2.45ab It resides in the anus, the penis, and the perineum; in the thighs, the scrotum, and the knees; 2.45cd as well as in the shanks, the abdomen, the hips, and the base of the navel.
2.46ab Vyāna, however, resides in the ears, the eyes, the middle of the neck, as well as in the ankles;
2.46cd in the nose, the throat, and the region of the eyes—it abides in these locations.
2.47ab The udāna wind resides in all the joints, as well as in the feet and the hands.
2.48ab The *samāna* wind is always situated in the body, pervading everything.
2.48cd It distributes all consumed flavors throughout the limbs together with the digestive fire (*vahni*).
2.49ab Moving through seventy-two thousand channels,
2.49cd the samāna wind alone remains pervading the entire body.
The five winds, beginning with *nāga*, are situated within the skin, bones, and other constituent parts.
Inhalation, exhalation, coughing, and so forth are considered the functions of the *prāṇa* wind;
the evacuation of feces, urine, and the like is the function of the *apāna* wind.
2.51ef The activities of abandoning, grasping, and so forth are proclaimed to be the function of the pervasive wind (vyāna).
2.52ab That which consists of the lifting up of the body and so forth is declared to be the function of udāna.
2.52cd The function of samāna in the body is proclaimed to be nourishment and the like.
2.53ab That quality which consists of belching and so forth is proclaimed as the function of Nāga;
2.53cd the closing of the eyes and so forth belongs to Kūrma, while sneezing belongs to Kṛkara.
2.54ab O best of brahmins, lassitude is proclaimed as the activity of Devadatta;
2.54cd for Dhananjaya, all activities such as emaciation and so forth are proclaimed.

2.55ab Having thus understood the configuration of the channels and the locations of the vital winds with diligence, 2.55cd one should perform the purification of the channels according to the prescribed rule.
2.56ab Engaged in the actions prescribed by the injunctions, he is free from all desires;
2.56cd endowed with the qualities such as self-restraint (yama) and the like, he is free from all attachments.
Then, having gone to a penance grove provided with fruits, roots, and water,
he should dwell there in a pleasant and pure place, by a river or even in a temple.
Having constructed a very beautiful monastery provided with all means of protection,
one should remain pure and composed, engaged in bathing at the three periods of the day.
2.59ab The steadfast one, whose body is consecrated with mantras and who always wears white ashes,
2.59cd should spread kuśa grass upon a soft seat, or else a horse-skin.
Having thoroughly worshipped Vināyaka with fruits, roots, water, and other offerings,
and having bowed to one's chosen deity and the Guru, one should take one's seat there and begin.
2.61ab One should sit facing either east or north, seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) oneself;
2.61cd with neck, head, and body held straight, the mouth closed, and remaining perfectly motionless.

2.62ab Having always properly placed the right hand upon the nose, [one should gaze at] the orb of the moon at the tip of the nose, overspread with a network of moonlight. 2.62cd–2.63ab [One should contemplate] the fourth letter of the seventh class, joined with the bindu.
Having observed that which resides in the center of the bindu with both eyes together with the mind;
2.64ab One should fill the breath with air from the outside through the *iḍā* for twelve *mātrās*.
2.64cd Then one should meditate on the fire as before, accompanied by a series of flickering flames.
Meditating on the letter *ra* joined with a bindu, situated within the circle of fire,
one should then exhale slowly through the *piṅgalā* channel.
2.66ab Again, having filled the breath from the right side with Piṅgalā, the wise one;
2.66cd then the intelligent person should exhale slowly through Iḍā.
2.67ab Or for three or four years, or even for three or four months; 2.67cd one should thus practice diligently six times during the three periods of the day.
2.68ab One attains the purification of the channels, characterized by distinct signs:
2.68cd lightness of the body, radiance, and the increase of the digestive fire.
2.69ab The manifestation of the sound (nāda) is the sign that indicates its purification.

For this [practice] consisting of the eight limbs is indeed purifying and a destroyer of sins.
O you whose wealth is austerity, this most secret and meritorious knowledge has been proclaimed to you.
For one who performs daily rites with this very knowledge,
being free from attachment to the fruits of action, liberation stands within his grasp.
Whoever recites this meritorious narrative daily with undistracted mind shall be liberated from all sins and become a knower of truth.
Furthermore, whoever listens to this daily, endowed with faith and devotion, [shall likewise attain the same].
Sin committed in a single lifetime is destroyed in a single day by one who hears this supreme narrative called Yoga even once,
or who reflects upon it correctly; such a person shall attain omniscience.
Those who, endowed with this knowledge, constantly perform these obligatory rites—

even the gods bow down upon seeing them engaged in their daily duties. Therefore, until the end of the body, one should perform the obligatory rites according to the prescribed rule through knowledge.
"O son, that which must be done by an embodied being who fears worldly existence for the sake of liberation [has been explained].
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Yoga Section of the Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā.
Chapter Five.
Thus addressed by the high-souled yogi Vasiṣṭha,
Śakti, the son of the yogi, questioned his illustrious father once again.
Śakti said:

If the Self is devoid of qualities, pure, eternally blissful, undecaying, and immortal, then, my dear father, whose would be the cycle of worldly existence? And when the field is destroyed, how could there be any remaining state? O Blessed Father, how is the time of its destruction known?
"You ought to tell me all of this correctly now.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Of that very Self, which is eternally pure and always composed of bliss..."
The wise proclaim that the transmigratory existence of the individual soul (jīva) is conditioned by limitations.
For indeed, the single Self of all beings resides within every being;
it appears as one and also as many, like the moon reflected in water.
That very Self, when mounted upon delusion, becomes known as the individual soul (jīva).

Because it discerns the field (kṣetra), it is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). It is declared to be the Knower of the Field because it experiences both the auspicious and the inauspicious.‖5.6‖

The object of enjoyment is both internal and external—such as pleasure and so forth, as well as jars and so forth—within this body, which is the locus of experience, by means of the senses, which are the instruments of enjoyment.
The enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, the act of enjoyment, and the sense-organ, which is the locus of enjoyment; || 5.7 ||
These are the five entities; a sixth entity does not exist. (5.8) Likewise, there are four states: waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
the fourth is called the "transcendental" (turīya), but there is no fifth state. (5.9)
Even in a dream, the enjoyment of an enjoyer who is empty of externality is proclaimed.
Deep sleep is the state of abiding in one's own essential nature, free from activity;
in that which is called the fourth (turiya), the self exists with the states of worldly existence destroyed. || 5.10–5.11 ||
Upon the destruction of the field, its persistence remains— whether in the aerial or the fiery [element]—
within this subtle *liṅga-śarīra* of the eternally undivided Self. That which is designated as the *jīva* exists everywhere by means of the *liṅga-deha*.
And by the power of merit and demerit, it assumes another body through that very same [cause].
In this very way, the individual soul wanders about as long as there is the exhaustion of karma;
from the exhaustion of karma comes the purification of the self, and by means of that purified [self], there is the realization of the Self.
Liberation occurs only through the power of meditative yoga and not otherwise;

however, the time for the destruction of the field is known by means of indicators that signal the time. Having understood this through internal and external signs, one should proceed according to one's inclination.
As long as one possesses a field (kṣetra), so long should one accomplish all that is to be achieved;
for when that is destroyed, who would be capable [of anything]? Indeed, the conjunction with a field is difficult to obtain.
Among beings, those with a field are superior; among those with a field, those who live by their intellect are superior.
Among the intelligent, men are considered the best; among men, the Brahmins;
among Brahmins, the learned; and among the learned, those whose intellects are perfected.
Among those with perfected intellects, the doers [of righteous deeds] are superior; and among doers, those who know Brahman.
For those who know Brahman, nothing superior to this exists here in this world. A twice-born man who possesses knowledge of the field (*kṣetra*) alone should act for his own supreme welfare;
by means of that, he should understand time through both external and internal signs.

Having recognized the time of death by these signs, one who is liberated shall go to the supreme goal. Listen now to the internal signs therein, which arise through the movement of the vital winds (vāyu):
the wind moves within this body through the portions of the moon and the sun.
Externally and internally within all beings, poison resides in the solar portion and nectar likewise in the lunar portion;
the moon and sun perpetually move through these two by the power of time. (5.22–5.23)
All are subject to time, for time alone is independent;
therefore, one should always correctly understand time from the very beginning by means of its signs, on both the left and the right sides. 5.24 savye ca dakṣiṇe cāpi pārśvayor ubhayor api |
The vital air (vāyu) circulates within the bodies of embodied beings in the form of breath.
Those who know time understand time here by means of the number of breaths:
sixty breaths constitute one prāṇa, and six prāṇas constitute one ghaṭikā.
Five ghaṭikās constitute one rāśi; twelve rāśis make a day.
Thirty days constitute a month, and two months become one season (ṛtu).
One should know that three seasons make an ayana, and likewise a viṣuva.

A year consists of six seasons; one hundred such years constitute the maximum lifespan. (5.28) Every day, together with the planets, twelve zodiac signs enter [the body] as twelve breaths; thus, for each single sign, there are exactly five nāḍīs. (5.29)
Aries and Taurus, Gemini and likewise Cancer;
Leo, Virgo, Libra, and Scorpio as well as Sagittarius;
Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces—these indeed are the zodiac signs.
The signs beginning with Aries are, in order, of the nature of movable, fixed, and dual.
They say that the four movable ones are in the left side;
the fixed ones would be in the south; and those of dual nature are in both.
The past, the present, and the future, as well as the fruits of the auspicious and inauspicious,
are to be understood within this body according to the rising of the planets in these zodiac signs (rāśis). Within each of these signs, there are five elements.
Wind, fire, earth, water, and space—these indeed are the five.
Among all the [elemental] groups, the first channel is that of wind;
the second channel is considered to be of fire; and the third is considered to be of earth.
The fourth is to be known as Vāruṇī, and the fifth is remembered as Vyomā (the Etherial).
The wind flows through the nostrils during the zodiacal signs belonging to the portion of Vāyu;
moving upward during the portion of Agni, it flows along the side of the pillar of Earth.
The wind flows through the lower part of the nose when the portion of Varuṇa is rising;
likewise, it flows through the middle of the nose in the element of space (vyoman) when the portion of space prevails.
Jupiter and Rāhu move in the northwest, while Venus and Mars move in the southeast.
On earth, Mercury and the Sun are to be known; in water, the Moon and Saturn; in the sky, one should find Mars. Thus it is for all the zodiac signs.
Those previously mentioned are auspicious everywhere, while those immediately following them are malefic.

Rāhu, Mars, the Sun, and Saturn—these are auspicious when situated to the south; Jupiter, Mercury, Venus, and the Moon—these gentle planets bring good fortune when on the left (north). However, malefic planets are auspicious when on the left, whereas these gentle planets yield malefic results [when on the right].‖5.40‖
All [planets] are auspicious during entry, but bring inauspiciousness during departure.

Thus, having understood the auspicious and inauspicious effects regarding the beings situated in the zodiac signs according to the rising of the planets, the wise man, when questioned, should then declare everything.
Wherever the wind is situated, if the querent is there, one should predict auspiciousness;
if he is situated where the wind is not present, his [inquiry] will be in vain.
The front is said to be the right side, and the back is declared to be the left. (5.43–5.44)
If the questioner stands in front [of the planet], the result is like that of the right side; for one standing behind it, the result is said to be like that of the left side.
[This applies to] eating, sexual union, battle, and likewise the accumulation of wealth.
One should perform these actions when Vāyu is situated in the south:
journeys, marriage rites, and whatever other auspicious deeds there may be—
all of these one should perform when Vāyu is established in the left.
If the wind is in the left [nostril], the wise man should not undertake a journey even if it is toward the fire [direction];
if he should go out of delusion, then even Brahmā cannot turn back.
However, when the wind is in the earth element or the portion of Varuṇa, going forth is a means for achieving happiness.
One should travel with effort even during a portion of the sky [at night], yet at some time,
if there is a reversal of the wind's rising during the first part of the day,
agitation of the mind will occur, and because of that, the failure of the task arises.
If, however, there is a contrary rising in the second house,
loss of wealth and suffering will occur immediately.
And if it is in the third house, there will be suffering during the journey.
In the fourth year there shall be loss of wealth; in the fifth, turmoil in the country.
In the sixth there shall be misfortune, and in the seventh the onset of disease.
One should know that in the eighth there is death, and in the ninth the destruction of the intellect.
In the tenth [house], there is bodily suffering; in the next, the loss of friends.
But in the final sign of the day, all manner of misconduct occurs.
Even when these signs are reversed in the positions of living beings, the same results follow.
"One should know that there will be fear from all living beings and misfortune from the king.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Yoga Section of the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā.
Chapter Six.
Śakti said: "By what means, O Blessed One, does one who knows time transcend time?
I wish to hear that; tell it to me correctly, O Lord. (6.1)
Thus questioned by Śakti, the proponent of the Vedas, the Blessed One looked upon his son with compassion and spoke of the means to victory. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having determined for himself the proper time through external and internal signs,
he— fearless, serene in soul, free from the pairs of opposites, and with senses conquered—
performs the obligatory and occasional rites prescribed by the injunctions.
Having reached the Supreme Self within the cave of the heart by means of yoga through the mind,
one whose vital breaths are conquered and who is free from desire should constantly mutter the Tāraka mantra;
or, being free from desire and steadfast on the path, he should mutter the Brahman that is the Tāraka.
"Having passed that time, one becomes long-lived and a knower of Brahman;
thus did Brahmā formerly explain the Praṇava to me in brief.
I shall declare that to you; listen, O high-minded son.
"O gentle one, in the beginning this was only Being (*sat*), the cause of birth and so forth.
From that cause arose the seed-syllable (*bīja*) consisting of the four *varṇas*, which is the syllable *oṃ*.
This very *oṃ* is Brahman, the sole means for the knowledge of Brahman. (6.8–6.9)

That by which the wise behold the omniscient, supreme nectar—that very abode of Brahman where the seers constantly perceive through their intellect within the *praṇava*—that I shall declare to you; listen. (6.10)
The consonant known as *saṃhāra* (the visarga) is half a mora in length;
that syllable is like the rising sun and is accompanied by a bindu.
That too is designated as *oṃkāra*; having conquered the breaths, one should meditate upon it with a concentrated mind.
This light of the heart is seen at the end of the letter *a* in the form of a drop (*bindu*).
Above the drop is the resonance (*nāda*), resembling pure crystal;
it illuminates the mind of the one whose consciousness is purified, within the power of the awakened faculty.
"In him dwells Rudra, the Great Seer, superior to the universe, dark-brown of hue, with vital energy drawn upward and three eyes; so say the scriptures.
Rudra alone is to be awakened by the ultimate teachings of the Āgamas, and no other. (6.14)

For one who desires to see that [reality] which is connected to the end of the scriptures, the nectar, and the dark-brown [Kṛṣṇapiṅgala], his very sight is the syllable Oṃ. Oṃ is its designator (vācaka), and Rudra, the imperishable nectar, is its designated (vācya).
Thus spoke the Self-Existent One, the seer of Dharma, who knows the conclusion of the Vedas.
Even the learned masters of Sāṃkhya and other systems, always established in the Praṇava,
behold Mahādeva above the Nāda with the eye of knowledge.
Even Vyāsa and others are praiseworthy when purified by these syllables of the *praṇava*;
they perceive the Bull-bannered Lord at the end of the *nāda* with their minds.
This applies even to those bound by the snares of *saṃsāra*, whether they be yogis or non-yogis.
I see no other medicine against death than the three-eyed Lord (Tryambaka).

He who, having realized through the end of the scriptures that [Lord] who is dark-brown, the nectar, and the syllable Om placed upon the crown of the head, should meditate upon Him and chant the Praṇava. || 6.19–6.20 ||
Within him, Mahādeva constantly reveals himself;
moreover, for yogins, Mahādeva himself dwells directly within their hearts.
As the Lord of the entire world and its Master, the All-consuming One, he grants them satisfaction.
The Blessed Lord Rudra, surrounded by ten million Rudras, is well-pleased.
Since this syllable Oṃ has arrived and remains in the presence of one whose mind is disciplined through yoga, you should likewise behold it thus upon his head.

Thus, having duly performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the treasury of Brahman— the supreme nectar situated within that treasury— along with its seer, meter, deity, and application, the Self of All himself became established in yoga. (6.24)
And you, having first performed the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma) according to the prescribed method— either with the Gāyatrī or the Praṇava— for the sake of purifying yourself,
and being one whose mind is purified, [should contemplate] the supreme nectar situated within the body of the syllable Oṃ.
Having realized this, one should place the imperishable syllable *oṃ* within this very body.

With his body consecrated by the mantras and wrapped in white ashes, the steadfast one—having withdrawn all effects into their respective causes—is like one who has already conquered the vital breaths (*asus*). || 6.26 ||
Having fixed the mind through yoga upon the supreme station of Viṣṇu, which is endowed with the four [states], within this body— the city of Brahman—
one perceives Rudra, whose form is supreme bliss, situated in the cave of the heart.
If one is free from desire in the cave of the heart and does not wish for rebirth again,
he should always chant with the *tāraka* [mantra] this Supreme Self, the embodiment of supreme bliss, who has entered the cave and is immortal.

Having passed beyond that time, he becomes long-lived and a knower of Brahman. O son, he who abandons his body while uttering the *praṇava* with his speech shall become Brahman itself; therefore, he too is a conqueror of time.
And such, O best of sages, is the means for conquering Time:
within the heart-lotus, which possesses eight petals, rises from the midst of the bulb;
it has a stalk twelve finger-breadths long and an opening four finger-breadths wide.
When the pericarp, together with its filaments, has been expanded by breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and enveloped by the rays of the moon emitting the essence of nectar—
[one perceives] Ṛta, Satya, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, who is dark-brown.
[He saw] Sadāśiva, whose semen is drawn up, who has diverse eyes and universal form;
the Great God with five faces, ten arms, and three eyes, resembling pure crystal, residing in the hearts of all beings. (6.34–6.35)

One should, with a well-concentrated mind, contemplate there a person bathed on all sides by thousands of streams of nectar flowing from the downward-facing head-lotus, which is joined with the sixteen meters. 6.36.
One who is free from desire, not falling away from the path, should mutter the mantra "Tryambaka"; or likewise, [one should meditate] upon the lotus of the heart,
complete with filaments and a pericarp, and endowed with the orbs of Fire, Sun, and Moon.

[He saw] the Lord, whose body was half Umā, the bestower of boons, the cause of the three [worlds], the three-eyed one with noble limbs, possessing four arms and three eyes, surrounded by moonbeams emitting the essence of nectar.
Resembling pure crystal, bestowing fearlessness upon all the worlds,
with limbs consecrated by nectar, and being the embodiment of supreme bliss—
one should conquer [the self] within one's own mind according to the rite of Tryambaka.
One should recite [the mantra] while performing the daily rites and the occasional ones.
O dear one, one should meditate upon Rudra himself within one's own self as the "Reviver of the Dead.
He who [meditates on] Rudra, the soul of the universe, whose form is supreme bliss—
With the verse beginning "Tryambaka," and with other [mantras], he should worship that which is established within his own self;
he too becomes a "sacrificer to the Self" (ātmayājī), as correctly declared by the wise.
[He sees] the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self.
"One who perceives thus would be a true sacrificer to the Self," so said Svāyambhuva.
He who constantly beholds with a pure mind the Supreme Self abiding within the self, whose form is supreme bliss— he truly sees.
He truly sees who sees the Self, whose form is supreme bliss, as abiding in all beings or established within his own self.
He who always abandons that which resides in his own body and worships that which is situated outside [is mistaken].
Having cast aside the jewel held in his own hand, he desires to acquire another.
Therefore, by worshipping one's own Self— which is non-dual and the embodiment of supreme bliss—
with the mantra "So 'ham Om," one becomes a conqueror of death.
But he who is unable [to worship] within his own self should always worship externally,
especially in a *liṅga* that has arisen spontaneously or one that has been installed;
or he may worship Sadāśiva with the *ṛc* beginning "Tryambaka" or with other [mantras].
Rudra, the great seer who transcends the universe, dark and tawny, with upward-directed vital energy and three eyes, reveals himself in the mind of that person—
though he may be impure and afraid of death at all times and in every condition. (6.50)
In all circumstances and in every place, one should mutter the *mṛtasaṃjīvanī* [mantra].
For men bound by the noose of *saṃsāra* who long for liberation,
I see no other remedy against death than that which belongs to Tryambaka.
Such, O best of sages, is the means for conquering Time:
[one must worship] Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, Vāsudeva, the unborn Hari,
the four-armed one of noble limbs, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Wearing a crown and armlets, with eyes like lotus petals,
lips resembling the inner petals of a lotus, and bestowing fearlessness upon all the worlds—
remembering him here in this city of Brahmā, within the center of the heart-lotus.
Remembering the god Nārāyaṇa with his inner self directed toward Him,
O dear son, he too— having conquered time— proceeded by the path prescribed by the rules;
or else, by practicing meditative absorption (samādhi), one may deceive the time that has arrived.
Concentration is said to be emptiness, devoid of all undertakings;
concentration is the state of equality between the individual self and the supreme self.
That emptiness, however, is to be understood as being unassociated with meditative absorptions and the like.

O son, he who constantly meditates through samādhi upon emptiness— which is free from all undertakings and liberated from both existence and non-existence— he too, by virtue of his distinction, shall become a knower of yoga who conquers death. (6.60–61)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Yoga Section of the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā. Vasiṣṭha said:
7.1 One should also examine, with a concentrated mind, the auspicious and inauspicious results pertaining to the solstices, as well as the time of death for all beings and for oneself.
7.2ab If the sun should be in the sign of Aries during the northern course, O son, in the remaining portions of the signs,
7.2cd one should know there will be famine, conflict among kings, and likewise fear for the kingdom.
7.3ab If the sun's transit occurs in the southeastern quarter (āgneyāṃśa), one should predict danger from fire.
7.3cd There will be famine, but the kingdom will be secure, free from disease, and fearless.
7.4ab When a lunar station (*tithi*) is born in an earthy (*pārthiva*) *yāna*, there is likewise no premature death among children.
7.4cd The kingdom shall have abundant food, be secure, free from disease, and live without fear.
When the sun enters the portion of Kāruṇa, the earth will abound with water;
together with its dharma and its people, it will be free from disease and free from suffering.
7.6ab If the *ayana* occurs in the sign of space (*ākāśa*), there will be total destruction.
7.6cd Likewise, there will be the loss of territory for kings, as well as the destruction of elephants, horses, and so forth.
7.7ab However, the middle two degrees in the portion of the Sun belong to Varuṇa and Pṛthivī.
7.7cd Those two which are the portions of malefic planets among them, they know to be the lowest.
7.8ab If the left [hand] falls on a portion of Varuṇa or a benefic portion, it is most excellent;
7.8cd but if it falls on a portion of Vyoman in either case, it will cause suffering during the transit.
7.9ab At the beginning of the year, when the northern solstice has occurred,
7.9cd the wind should immediately flow through the right [nostril] for five *nāḍikās*.
7.10ab If the wind flows through five channels on the left side, he should be known as one who will live for a hundred years; if it is otherwise, his life will be short.
7.11ab It is said that for one whose [vital breath] flows for six ghaṭikās, his lifespan is eighty years. 7.11cd For one who has seven ghaṭikās, he attains a lifespan of sixty years.
7.12ab If the wind moves for eight ghaṭikās, one should indicate that his lifespan is fifty years. 7.12cd If it moves for nine ghaṭikās, the rule is that the lifespan is thirty-three years.
7.13ab If the wind flows for ten *ghaṭīs*, it is recorded that one will live for twenty-eight years;
7.13cd if the wind flows for half a day, one will live for twenty-five years.
7.14ab He for whom [the breath] flows in the left for a day lives for twelve years.
7.14cd He for whom it flows for a day and night lives for ten years.
If the wind flows for two days, one lives for eight years;
if the wind moves for three days, one lives for six years.
If the wind should blow for four days, one lives for four years;
if the wind should blow for five nights, his lifespan is three years.
If the wind flows for ten nights, death will occur after two years;
if it flows for fifteen days, his lifespan shall be one year.
7.18ab His lifespan is twenty days, and he experiences six months [of life].
7.18cd He experiences twenty-five nights and has a lifespan of three months.
7.19ab For one who has twenty-six days [remaining], death shall occur after two months.
If the wind [flows] for twenty-seven [days], he lives for one month.
7.20ab If there are twenty-eight days, his life will last for half a month;
7.20cd if there are twenty-nine, he lives for ten nights.
If the wind flows for thirty days, he lives for five nights;
if it flows for thirty-one days, death shall occur after three nights.
7.22ab They say that for one in whom thirty-two [vāyus] flow, there will be death within two days. 7.22cd If thirty-three should flow, his death occurs after one day.

7.23cd However, starting from the time of the solstice, one should indeed observe [the wind] as it moves toward the south.

7.25cd One should examine the movement of one's own vital breath (vāyu) in every season.
7.26ab Even the time of death must be known by those most skilled in yoga;
7.26cd beginning from the last five days of the transit [of the sun] in the month of Māgha.
7.27ab If the wind blows toward the south for him, his life lasts three years.
7.27cd Starting from the solar transit (saṃkrānti) of the month of Caitra, for five days...
7.28ab If the wind blows in the southern direction, his life lasts for six years.
7.28cd Starting from the solar transit (saṃkrānti) of the month of Jyeṣṭha, [this applies] for five days.
7.29ab For one in whom the wind blows toward the south, his lifespan is nine years.
7.29cd This begins from the fifth day after the solar transit (saṃkrānti) of Śrāvaṇa.
7.30ab He in whose [nostril] the wind blows toward the south lives for twelve years.
7.30cd Starting from the solar transit (saṃkrānti) of Āśvina, however, for five days...
7.31ab For one in whom the wind flows through the southern [channel], his life span is fifteen years. 7.31cd Starting from the transit (saṃkrānti) of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, for five days.

7.32ab If one’s wind flows in the southern [channel] for a limit of eighteen years, 7.32cd and if the vital air flows in that same manner in the left side as well, [one will live for twenty-four years].
7.33ab A various kind of fear other than death is proclaimed for him; 7.33cd immediately after the equinoctial time has occurred at the beginning of Aries and so forth.
7.34ab For one ghaṭikā, the wind flows in the right [nostril] from the region of space (ākāśa).
7.34cd Thereafter, it naturally shifts to the left for all [beings].
7.35ab Through inversion, there shall be misfortune for all living beings as well.
7.35cd At that time of the equinox, however, [it occurs] on the left side from the northwestern direction.
7.36ab If the wind blows in such a manner, famine and other calamities will occur.
7.36cd This shall happen at the beginning of the bright fortnight of whichever month it may be.
Likewise, the wise man should examine death by means of the movement of the breaths.
7.37cd At the beginning of the lunar day, wind arises for three days in the moon;
7.37ef then for three days in the sun, then in the moon, and then in the sun.
7.38ab Even Kṛṣṇa said this at the beginning of the day: when the sun is in the moon, and likewise when it is in the sun;
7.38cd one should know that the rising of the wind occurs when the moon is in the sun.
7.39ab When there is a reversal of these three during the arising of the three phases,
7.39cd the wise man should then announce death within half a day.

7.39ef If it blows for two fortnights, there will be the destruction of the earth; if for one fortnight, there will be mental anguish. 7.39gh If it should blow for half a fortnight, strife and the like will occur.
7.39ij If the wind should blow toward the south for one day, and likewise [for] always [the same duration].
7.39k Death occurs after three years; 7.39m death after two days or two years;
7.39n death after three days or ten months; and death after one month.
7.40ab If, O gentle one, death should thus blow for only a single day in a month,
7.40cd there will be disease, loss of wealth, distress, anger, and conflict.
If it should likewise move on both sides, the result is said to be like that of Yāmya; if it should flow to the left for half a day, then there will be the destruction of one's wealth.
7.42ab When the movement is toward the south during the period of equal motion, there is great calamity.
7.42cd One should examine the course of Vāyu during the yoga known as Sāvitra.
7.43ab Furthermore, the time of death must be known by those most skilled in yoga.
7.43cd If the moon is situated in the seventh zodiac sign from the sun, [death is imminent].
7.44ab When the breath is situated there in the birth-constellation, it is called the Sāvitra yoga.
7.44cd If, at that time, the wind should flow in one place for half a day, [it is so].
7.45ab His death will occur when he reaches his fourteenth year.
7.45cd This applies to one for whom the Sāvitra-yoga begins and continues in the same [lunar day] for an entire day.
O Sage, at the end of twelve years he goes to the abode of Yama;
for him, the life span is ten years, during which the wind flows for one day and night.
7.47ab For one in whom the Sāvitra yoga begins and the vital breath flows in a single location for two days, 7.47cd his life is said to last until the end of eight years.
7.48ab For one in whom the vital breath flows for three consecutive days, beginning from the *sāvitra* yoga, 7.48cd his lifespan is proclaimed to end within six years.
7.48ef–48gh: For one who, beginning with the Sāvitra-yoga, maintains the breath in a single location for four days, it is said that their lifespan extends to the end of four years.
7.49ab Starting from the conjunction with Savitṛ for five days along a single path,
7.49cd it is said that death will come after three years for one in whom the wind flows [thus].
7.50ab Having undertaken this yoga, one should maintain it for six days at a time; 7.50cd his lifespan will be three years minus twenty-four days.
7.51ab Having begun this yoga, one should maintain it for seven days in solitude.
7.51cd His life will be three years less seventy-two days.
Having begun this yoga, one should carry it out for eight days;
his lifespan is two and a half years plus twenty-six [additional days].
7.53ab Having begun this yoga, one should practice it for nine days on one side.
7.53cd His lifespan will be two years plus four months.
7.54ab Having begun this yoga, one should observe it for ten days on one side.
7.54cd For him whose breath [flows thus] at that time, one should know his life span to be two years.
If [the breath] flows for one whose [counting] has begun on the eleventh day,
his life will last for two years minus twenty-four days.
7.56ab If one maintains this yoga for twelve days,
7.56cd his life will last for two years minus seventy-two days.
If one undertakes this yoga on the thirteenth day [of the lunar fortnight],
he lives for one year and a half, plus twenty-six [days].
7.58ab Having begun this yoga, one should carry it for fourteen days.
7.58cd O child, his lifespan shall be a year plus four months.
7.59ab Likewise, if the wind should blow continuously from one side for fifteen days; 7.59cd death shall occur at the end of the year for that person whose wind [blows thus].
If one maintains this yoga for sixteen days after beginning it,
his lifespan shall be sufficient for a full year minus twelve years.
If, starting from that [day], one should flow for seventeen days on one side alone,
it will certainly become known as the "Yama" [wind] when twenty-six years have been subtracted from one's lifespan.
If the wind flows starting from that [day] for eighteen days,
death shall occur at the end of the year minus seventy-two days.
If death occurs for one after nineteen days from the seventh month,
it is proclaimed that for one [who dies] after twenty days, the lifespan is six months.
If [the breath] flows from one side for twenty-one days starting from a certain point,
death will occur within half a year minus eleven days.
If [the breath] flows from one side for twenty-two days starting from that point,
death will occur in half a year when eighteen days of this [period] have elapsed.
7.64ab Starting from that [point], one should calculate for twenty-three nights on one side;
7.64cd when this [period] is reduced by twenty-six days, death occurs within half a year.
Starting from that [moment], one should carry it for twenty-four nights;
its life is proclaimed to last exactly four months.
7.66ab Starting from that [point], one should observe it for twenty-five nights;
7.66cd the death of such a person is proclaimed by the learned to occur after three months.
If the wind flows in one place for twenty-six days,
his death is proclaimed by the learned to occur within two months.
If the wind flows in a single location for twenty-seven nights,
death at the end of that month is proclaimed by the learned.
If the wind flows in one place for twenty-eight nights,
death is proclaimed to occur at the end of twenty-five days.
If the wind (māruta) should flow in a single location for twenty-nine days,
his death is proclaimed by the learned to occur after ten days.
When the vital wind (māruta) begins to flow for thirty days starting from the seventh day, his destruction occurs within five days; there is no doubt in this matter.
If the vital wind flows in a single channel for thirty-one days, his death will occur after three days; this has been proclaimed by the learned.
If the wind flows in one [nostril] for thirty-two days, death will occur for that person after two days; this has been proclaimed by the learned.
If the wind flows in a single location for thirty-three days,
death for that person is proclaimed by the learned to occur after one day.
7.72ab If the wind should blow thus on the left side during the aforementioned times,
7.72cd that is proclaimed by the learned as bringing anxiety regarding disease.
The wise have declared that there is danger from the loss of sons and friends, as well as from famine and the like, and furthermore, cruel fear of the king.
7.74ab Sitting comfortably in a secluded place, one should examine what is auspicious and what is inauspicious.
7.74cd Otherwise, it becomes fruitless; so it has been proclaimed by the wise.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Yoga-kāṇḍa of the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā. Vasiṣṭha said:
8.1ab Furthermore, I shall describe to you many kinds of external signs of death; 8.1cd listen now, my son, to all those indications.
8.2ab He who sees smoke above his own head during the two twilights,
8.2cd and perceives it for five days, will die within three years.
If death should occur after four days, it will happen within two years;
if it should occur after three days, his death will occur within one year.
If one observes swinging during both external twilights,
or if the *brahmasūtra* (the central line) is destroyed, death will come for him within a year.
If, when both ears are covered with the hands, the internal sound of the body is no longer heard for one year,
his death will occur.
8.5ab If there is a simultaneous disappearance from both positions,
8.5cd or if there is a destruction of the *brahmasūtra*, his [death] will occur within a year.
8.6ab For one who experiences sudden obesity or sudden emaciation,
8.6cd or excessive anger or excessive fear, even that person's destruction will occur within a year.
If these— feces, urine, hunger, and exhaustion— should arise simultaneously,
then his death will occur within that month, on that lunar day, in that year.
If one should see a city of Gandharvas atop a tree anywhere,
one should foresee his death within a year.
8.9ab If, moreover, one's own body suddenly appears blackish-brown,
8.9cd one should foresee his death occurring within a year.
8.10ab If one's body is devoured by vultures, dogs, crows, jackals, donkeys, camels, or cranes, 8.10cd his death will occur within a year.
8.11ab Even if one's own body should be seen as devoured by these [beings] even in a dream, 8.11cd death will occur for him within a year; of this there is no doubt.
8.12ab One who is touched by Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, and the like, shall meet death within one year.
8.12cd [One should not look at] Arundhatī, Dhruva, the shadow of the moon (Soma-chāyā), or the Great Path (Mahāpatha).
8.13ab He who does not see [the reflection] will undoubtedly die within a year.
8.13cd Or, if he sees his own private parts while devoid of shame, [he will likewise die].
8.14ab Even he who goes to the great abode within a year, of this there is no doubt;
8.14cd [it is as impossible as] the sun or the moon falling from the sky while deprived of their luster.
8.15ab For one who sees this, death shall occur even before half a year has passed.
8.15cd If, amidst the stars, there is no stalk [of light], and his lips and palate are parched;
8.16ab O son, there is no doubt that his death will occur after half a year, if the moon cannot be seen through the space between two fingers.
8.16cd If the moon cannot be seen through the space between two fingers, [then this shall happen].
8.17ab He whose three fingers [of the hand] are thus [curved] shall meet death within half a year.
8.17cd Furthermore, thousands [of worms] come toward him as his body becomes crooked.
8.18ab And when those [omens] are not seen, he too shall meet death within six months;
8.18cd his body licked by crows and vultures, and smeared with the scent of blood.
Anointed with oil, extremely terrified, shaven-headed, and wearing red garments,
he mounted a hand and rushed with speed toward the southern direction.
8.20ab For one whose own self is seen in a dream, death occurs after half a year;
8.20cd or if the sound of a bell should be heard at the conclusion of sexual intercourse.
8.21ab His death shall occur before half a year; there is no doubt in this.
8.21cd One who possesses two forms may see a chameleon moving in the sky.
8.22ab He whose footprint should appear broken in mud or even in dust will meet his death before half a year has passed.
8.23ab His death shall occur before half a year; there is no doubt in this.
8.23cd If one does not see [the sun] like a firefly when it is pressed by the fingers, [death is near].
8.24ab If he sees [the signs] even when his eyes are not being pressed, death shall occur for him within half a year. 8.24cd [This applies] even if the eyes themselves are not being afflicted.
If [the deity] has the color and brilliance of a firefly, death is said to occur in three months;
[if it is] black, holding an iron staff, and clad in black garments and equipment.
If he perceives these in a dream, his death will occur within three months;
likewise, if the sense faculties do not grasp their respective objects.
8.27ab At the end of the month, his death will occur; of this there is no doubt. 8.27cd He whose head falters and who sees meteors in the sky [shall likewise die].
8.28ab If a rainbow appears at night, or if one's head should suddenly blaze; 8.28cd or if lightning strikes even when there are no clouds—he too shall die within a month.
8.29ab He who does not see his own reflection in a mirror or in water, 8.29cd for him too death will occur within a month; of this there is no doubt.
8.30ab Or he may see sexual intercourse, or crows, swans, and peacocks; 8.30cd when [he sees] things that are neither too cold nor too hot, he will die within a month.
8.31ab Even for one whose heart and feet wither away merely by bathing, 8.31cd death will occur at the end of a month; of this there is no doubt.
If the rays of the sun were cold and the rays of the moon were hot, even he would go to the abode of Yama within half a month; of this there is no doubt.
8.33ab He who suddenly sees a hole in the earth, or even a hole in the sun; 8.33cd his death will occur within three months, of this there is no doubt.

8.34ab If the face resembles a red lotus and the tongue has the luster of collyrium; 8.34cd likewise, if the limbs repeatedly exhibit that same appearance, he too shall meet death within half a month.
8.35ab If one experiences trembling of the heart and navel, as well as trembling of the palate, 8.35cd one should know that his death will occur within half a month; of this there is no doubt.
8.36ab For him upon whose body a sudden flame arises while burning, 8.36cd he goes to the abode of death within seven days; of this there is no doubt.
He who does not see the seven planets and the Seven Sages (the Great Bear) in a cloudless sky,
and whose sense of smell and taste have also failed, shall meet death within seven days.
8.38ab If one half of his body is hot and the other half is excessively cold,
or if there is a loss of memory regarding past actions, he will die within seven days.
8.39ab If the corners of his eyes are drawn inward and devoid of luster,
or if his nose becomes crooked, he will not live for seven nights.
8.40ab If one's own shadow appears deformed, or if there is the dragging of teeth;
8.40cd or if the odor of a corpse arises suddenly, his life will last but three nights.
8.41ab But he who sees his own shadow situated to the south while standing in the north, 8.41cd will meet with destruction immediately; there is no doubt about this.
If the food of such a person is ever eaten by a woman, his death will occur immediately; of this there is no doubt.
8.43ab He who, at the time of eating, should see the one whose vehicle is a bull in the midst of the sky,
8.43cd or should see another holding a staff— he too shall die immediately.
And if at the time of eating one should see a woman with disheveled red hair, likewise holding a noose, he too shall die immediately.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Yoga Section of the Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā.
